# Venue record: NeurIPS 2026, Main Track (contribution type "General")

Sources: `ht-role venue neurips` (the world's venue library, retrieved 2026-11-14 from neurips.cc pages and the official style kit) and, for contribution types, https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2026/ReviewerGuidelines (fetched 2026-11-25). Section "Accepted papers" below is my own measurement (`tools/`). Everything else is quoted or paraphrased from those sources; where I recommend something the venue does not require, it says **recommendation**.

## 1. Choice of venue

The objective lets the study pick one of ICML, ICLR, NeurIPS and requires the newest edition's official template and checklist. I pick **NeurIPS 2026 Main Track** (newest NeurIPS edition with a published call; NeurIPS 2027 pages return HTTP 404 on 2026-11-14, so the edition and its template are the 2026 ones).

Why not the others (from the same library):

| | NeurIPS 2026 | ICML 2027 | ICLR 2027 |
|---|---|---|---|
| main-text limit | 9 pages, floats included | 8 pages | 9 pages |
| layout | one column, 5.5 in text width | two columns, 6.75 in text width, 3.25 in columns | one column, 5.5 in |
| checklist | mandatory, in the kit (`checklist.tex`), outside the page limit | none in the library record | none; an optional reproducibility statement |

The outline plans eight main figures and two tables; a single-column 9-page body is the best fit, and the NeurIPS paper checklist is the one the objective names as an example. A switch would change page budget and widths below; ask me first.

**Contribution type: choose "General"** (reviewers read criteria by the type the authors select; it cannot be changed after submission). "Negative Results" is for papers whose main contribution is understanding a negative result and has a *higher* significance and originality bar ("unexpected or surprising", "changes our understanding of an important question", and not "simply an empirical observation that some experiment did not turn out as expected"). The study's thesis (an extrapolation account of regression-GATE error, a regime map, a diagnostic) is evaluation-of-existing-methods work, which the General originality criterion names explicitly ("new insights, deepen understanding, or highlight important properties of existing methods"). If results reverse the thesis into a pure negative finding, tell me and reconsider.

## 2. What the venue requires

### Length and structure
- Main text: **at most 9 content pages, including all figures and tables**. Not counted: references, acknowledgments, technical appendices, the paper checklist. Over the limit: "will not be reviewed" (kit) / may be desk rejected (handbook). Camera-ready gets 10 pages; submission is the standard here.
- References, appendix and checklist have no page limit. Order inside the single PDF (suggested by the handbook): content, references, appendices, checklist. The paper must stand alone without the appendix; reviewers are not required to read appendix or supplement.
- Required sections: none fixed by the venue. The objective (not the venue) requires abstract, introduction, related work, method, experiments, discussion and limitations, references.
- A broader-impacts section is not required; any societal-impact discussion inside the paper counts against the 9 pages.

### Layout (enforced by `neurips_2026.sty`; do not edit it, "tweaking the style files may be grounds for desk rejection")
- US Letter; one column; text block 5.5 in wide x 9 in high; left margin 1.5 in, top 1 in; Times 10 pt on 11 pt leading; paragraphs unindented, 5.5 pt apart; page numbers on.
- `\footnotesize` is floored at 8 pt, `\scriptsize` at 7 pt, `\tiny` at 6 pt by the style. References may use `\small` (9 pt). Do not load `fullpage`/`geometry` tricks, do not shrink margins or fonts.
- Submission mode (no `final`/`preprint` option): anonymous author block, line numbers (do not refer to them), footer "Submitted to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing S

**Abstract:** I can't reproduce the full abstract word for word, because my quoting limit is 125 characters per quote. You can read it in full on the arXiv page (2309.07476). Here is a summary with short quotes.

The paper opens by saying "Network experiments are powerful tools for studying spillover effects". It argues that regression-based point estimates and standard errors can have solid theoretical guarantees when the regression functions and robust standard errors are specified to fit the interference patterns. It notes that "the Hájek estimator is numerically identical to the coefficient from the weighted-least-squares fit", where the weights come from the inverse probability of the exposure mapping. It lists three advantages of the regression approach: easy implementation, standard errors from the same fit, and the option to add covariates for efficiency. Finally, it says "the regression-based network-robust covariance estimator can be anti-conservative under nonconstant effects", so the authors propose an adjusted covariance estimator to improve coverage.

**Estimand:** The abstract never names the estimand outright. It points to spillover effects defined through an exposure mapping, meaning contrasts in average outcomes between units under different exposure conditions. The Hájek estimator and the weighted least squares fit target these.

**Assumptions (as far as the abstract shows):**
- Treatments are randomly assigned over the network, so inference is design-based and avoids endogeneity.
- Interference is summarized by an exposure mapping, and exposure probabilities are used as weights.
- No strong outcome-modeling assumptions are imposed.
- Treatment effects may be nonconstant, which is why the covariance adjustment is needed.

The abstract gives no further formal detail, such as the exact exposure mapping or regularity conditions, so those would have to come from the full paper.

I can't give the full abstract verbatim, because my quotes are capped at 125 characters. Here is a condensed version with short exact quotes.

**Paper:** arXiv:2405.15887, by Thiyageswaran, McCormick, and Brennan.

- **Problem:** "Randomized controlled trials often suffer from interference," meaning one unit's treatment changes its neighbors' outcomes. This biases simple estimates of the average treatment effect.
- **Existing approach:** The Horvitz-Thompson estimator is paired with an exposure mapping. One example mapping sets a cutoff *h*, the fraction of a unit's neighbors that share its treatment status. The cutoff is hard for domain experts to specify, and a wrong choice introduces bias.
- **Contribution:** The authors pick *h* from the data so that it "minimizes the mean squared error of the Hortvitz-Thompson estimator." They estimate bias and variance at each candidate threshold using a linear dose-response model of potential outcomes.
- **Evidence:** Simulations show gains over fixed threshold choices. The authors also run experiments on a public Amazon product similarity graph.
- **Robustness:** They report that "our method is robust to deviations from the linear potential outcomes model."

For the complete abstract text, see the arXiv page directly.

I can't give the full abstract word for word, because quotes are capped at 125 characters. Here is a version that mixes short exact quotes with paraphrase.

**Abstract (arXiv:1808.08683, Alex Chin)**

- "Standard estimators of the global average treatment effect can be biased in the presence of interference."
- The paper offers regression-based corrections for Bernoulli randomized experiments to remove that bias.
- The approach: "We use a fitted model to predict the counterfactual outcomes of global control and global treatment."
- It departs from ordinary regression adjustment because the covariates are built from functions of the treatment assignment vector. Researchers can use any functions related to the outcome, so spotting interference becomes a feature-engineering task.
- The author derives the estimator's distribution under a linear model and relates it to classical regression adjustment theory under SUTVA.
- A further estimator accommodates flexible machine learning models for nonlinear interference.
- Inference relies on bootstrap and resampling, which avoids modeling the complex dependence from interference. It needs an exogeneity assumption similar to unconfoundedness in observational studies.
- In simulations, the methods remove bias better than inverse-propensity-weighted estimators based on neighborhood exposure modeling.
- The application is a reanalysis of a study on "weather insurance adoption" among villages in rural China.

For the complete original text, see the abstract on the arXiv page.

The skeleton and the related-work section are on `dev`; the rest of the paper waits for results.

- **Venue:** `venue-repo` chose NeurIPS 2026, main track, contribution type "General". The limit is 9 content pages including figures and tables. Its recommendation is at most 6 figures and 2 tables in the main text.
- **Anonymity:** the paper must not name repositories, roles or hosts. Reproduction details belong in the released code, so the paper says only once where it is released.
- **Skeleton:** the template and checklist are in `paper/`, with one file per section under `paper/sections/`. The bibliography is in `paper/refs.bib`. The build declaration is `.forgejo/document.json`. A local build with the checklist included gives 8 pages and no unresolved citations.
- **Related work:** I wrote this from the abstracts I fetched plus idea-repo's notes on the full texts. Those notes say Chin 2019, Han–Ugander 2023 and Gao–Ding 2023 were read by keyword and section, not in full. I stated the extrapolation viewpoint as not new, as the brief requires. I did not read the other cited sources.
- **Not done:** the abstract, introduction, method, design, results and discussion are empty, and the checklist still has its template placeholders. I fill them from the delivered results once `experiment-repo` and `figtab-repo` deliver.

I'll wake when they deliver.
